summary.text: Working modulo \(283411^2\), modular exponentiation gives \(28341^{28341}\equiv1\), while a finite computation shows that \(28341^d-1\) is coprime to the modulus for every proper divisor \(d\mid28341\). Since \(\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(n)=n^n-1\) and each proper-divisor cyclotomic value divides the corresponding \(n^d-1\), all those factors are units, forcing the remaining factor \(\Phi_{28341}(28341)\) to vanish modulo \(283411^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
n=28341,\qquad p=283411,\qquad M=p^2=80,321,794,921.
\]
Write \(\Phi_m(X)\) for the \(m\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. We will prove that
\[
M\mid \bigl|\Phi_n(n)\bigr|.
\]
Since \(M=p^2\), this is exactly the assertion that \(283411^2\) divides \(a(28341)\).

We work in the commutative ring
\[
R=\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z
\]
and denote by \(x\) the residue class of \(n=28341\) in this ring. An integer is divisible by \(M\) if and only if its residue class in \(R\) is zero. Thus it is enough to prove
\[
\Phi_n(x)=0\quad\text{in }R.
\]
Here, as usual, evaluating the reduction modulo \(M\) of an integral polynomial gives the same result as first evaluating the polynomial in \(\mathbb Z\) and then reducing the answer modulo \(M\).

We first record the finite modular calculations that will be needed. All of them can be performed by repeated squaring. The successive residues of \(n^{2^k}\) modulo \(M\), for \(0\leq k\leq14\), are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
k&2^k&n^{2^k}\pmod M\\ \hline
0&1&28,341\\
1&2&803,212,281\\
2&4&10,305,286,175\\
3&8&56,856,623,504\\
4&16&11,119,560,660\\
5&32&34,823,658,856\\
6&64&7,305,860,158\\
7&128&72,720,565,854\\
8&256&77,339,958,728\\
9&512&48,530,202,121\\
10&1024&18,484,540,212\\
11&2048&77,970,117,019\\
12&4096&39,630,026,099\\
13&8192&23,437,256,541\\
14&16384&8,780,247,748
\end{array}
\]
Each row after the first is obtained by squaring the preceding residue and reducing modulo \(M\).

Now
\[
28341=1+4+16+32+128+512+1024+2048+8192+16384.
\]
Multiplying the corresponding entries of the table modulo \(M\) gives, successively,
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
\text{largest newly included power of }2&\text{accumulated residue}\pmod M\\ \hline
1&28,341\\
4&12,069,152,919\\
16&58,902,886,234\\
32&3,524,814,247\\
128&59,346,352,675\\
512&71,235,197,045\\
1024&8,309,007,975\\
2048&79,405,617,822\\
8192&20,736,622,302\\
16384&1
\end{array}
\]
Consequently,
\[
x^{28341}=1\quad\text{in }R. \tag{1}
\]

Next we show that \(x^d-1\) is a unit in \(R\) for every proper positive divisor \(d\) of \(n\). Factorization gives
\[
28341=3^2\cdot47\cdot67.
\]
Therefore the positive divisors of \(28341\) are
\[
1,3,9,47,67,141,201,423,603,3149,9447,28341,
\]
and the first eleven are precisely the proper divisors.

For every proper divisor \(d\), let \(s_d\) be the least nonnegative residue of \(n^d-1\) modulo \(M\). Repeated squaring using the preceding powers gives the values in the second column of the following table. The third and fourth columns give integers \(u_d,q_d\) satisfying the exact integer identity
\[
s_du_d=1+q_dM.
\]
Thus the residue class of \(u_d\) is an explicit multiplicative inverse of \(x^d-1\) in \(R\).
\[
\begin{array}{r|r|r|r}
d&s_d&u_d&q_d\\ \hline
1&28,340&9,293,407,394&3,279\\
3&32,771,293,177&76,798,059,603&31,333,609,130\\
9&38,038,816,682&16,577,180,451&7,850,625,461\\
47&46,050,599,116&17,367,511,994&9,957,251,743\\
67&64,167,197,782&39,179,483,201&31,299,570,061\\
141&19,846,411,589&57,398,135,213&14,182,290,336\\
201&78,719,561,964&14,928,936,893&14,631,139,331\\
423&35,902,418,326&24,315,047,651&10,868,395,225\\
603&47,785,530,574&58,050,462,399&34,535,734,025\\
3149&55,540,222,233&29,648,934,674&20,501,389,721\\
9447&38,862,320,388&67,367,688,124&32,594,698,391
\end{array}
\]
For example, the meaning of each row is simultaneously that
\[
n^d-1\equiv s_d\pmod M
\]
and that
\[
s_du_d\equiv1\pmod M.
\]
It follows that
\[
x^d-1\text{ is a unit of }R
\quad\text{for every proper divisor }d\mid n. \tag{2}
\]

We now apply the cyclotomic factorization. For every positive integer \(m\),
\[
X^m-1=\prod_{d\mid m}\Phi_d(X).
\]
This identity has integral coefficients and therefore remains true over \(R\). Evaluating it at \(x\), with \(m=n\), gives
\[
\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)=x^n-1.
\]
By (1), the right-hand side is zero, so
\[
\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)=0. \tag{3}
\]

It remains to show that every factor in (3), except possibly the factor indexed by \(n\), is a unit. Fix a proper divisor \(d\mid n\). The cyclotomic factorization with exponent \(d\) says
\[
X^d-1=\prod_{e\mid d}\Phi_e(X).
\]
In particular, \(\Phi_d(X)\) divides \(X^d-1\) as a polynomial over \(\mathbb Z\), and hence also after reducing coefficients to \(R\). Evaluating at \(x\), we find that \(\Phi_d(x)\) divides \(x^d-1\) in \(R\). Thus there is some \(c_d\in R\) such that
\[
x^d-1=\Phi_d(x)c_d.
\]
By (2), the left side is a unit. In any commutative ring, a divisor of a unit is itself a unit: if \(ab\) has inverse \(v\), then \(a\) has inverse \(bv\). Therefore
\[
\Phi_d(x)\text{ is a unit in }R
\quad\text{for every proper divisor }d\mid n. \tag{4}
\]

Separate the factor corresponding to \(d=n\) in (3). We obtain
\[
\Phi_n(x)\prod_{\substack{d\mid n\\d<n}}\Phi_d(x)=0.
\]
By (4), every factor in the second product is a unit, and hence their product is a unit. Multiplication by its inverse cancels that product and yields
\[
\Phi_n(x)=0\quad\text{in }R.
\]
Therefore the integer \(\Phi_n(n)\) is congruent to zero modulo \(Miangle"]; hence
\[
M\mid \Phi_n(n).
\]
Divisibility by a positive integer is unaffected by changing an integer to its absolute value, so
\[
283411^2=M\mid \bigl|\Phi_{28341}(28341)\bigr|=a(28341).
\]
This proves the claim.
